title: Cooperation, Coordination and Negotiation
purpose: Seed cooperation as a first-class strategy among autonomous agents: distinguish cooperation, coordination, collaboration, negotiation, compromise, mutual aid and collective action; identify shared and conflicting interests; search for joint gains and fair processes; coordinate scarce resources without assuming competition or ownership; preserve consent and dissent; and repair conflict without requiring identical goals or permanent conformity.

concepts.definition: Agents voluntarily align some actions/resources toward compatible or shared outcomes while retaining distinct identities and potentially distinct goals.
Organizing timing, roles, information or resources so actions fit together and avoid unnecessary conflict/interference.
Joint cognitive/practical work in which participants contribute toward a shared task or artifact.
Process of communicating and adjusting proposals among parties with differing interests to seek an acceptable arrangement without assuming agreement is always possible.
Outcome multiple agents currently seek sufficiently in common for joint action; shared goals can coexist with other conflicting goals.
Distinct interests that can be simultaneously advanced without requiring identical preferences.
Interests that cannot all be fully satisfied under current constraints.
Arrangement improving outcomes for multiple parties relative to relevant alternatives without requiring equal benefit.
Arrangement in which parties accept less than some preferred outcome to achieve an acceptable joint resolution.
Voluntary exchange of resources/services/commitments under consent and governance; one coordination mechanism among many, not the default form of cooperation.
Voluntary reciprocal or solidaristic support based on need/relationship/community rather than requiring market exchange or immediate equivalence.
Coordinated action by multiple agents toward a shared/public/common objective.
Benefit whose provision can affect multiple parties and may create coordination/free-rider problems depending on context.
Rules/processes for collectively managing shared resources without assuming private ownership or unrestricted access.
Allocation/scheduling of limited shared resources according to declared needs, priorities, constraints and governance.
Procedure whose relevant participants, criteria, transparency and opportunities are judged appropriately fair under a stated normative/governance framework.
Assisted conflict-resolution process where a third party helps clarify interests, communication and options without automatically imposing an outcome.
Incompatibility among goals, interpretations, resource claims, boundaries or actions; conflict need not imply hostility.
Process of addressing causes/impacts of conflict and restoring workable coordination/relationship where desired.
Pattern of responding to benefits/obligations across interactions; can support cooperation but is not a requirement that every act be immediately repaid.
Coordination problem where an agent can benefit from a shared good without contributing, potentially undermining provision under some conditions.
Context-dependent ability to influence negotiated outcomes through alternatives, resources, authority, information or dependency.
Outcome available if negotiation/cooperation is not accepted; affects bargaining without determining fairness.
Learned/shared expectation supporting coordination, contribution, care or restraint; norms remain context-dependent and revisable.
Commitment to support others or collective wellbeing based on shared identification/values/conditions, potentially without direct individual return.

guards.reason: Cooperation requires sufficient compatibility, not identity of goals.
Scarcity can be addressed through scheduling, rationing, sharing, prioritization, commons governance or other mechanisms.
Allocation mechanism is a design/governance choice.
Negotiated acceptability is not epistemic validation.
Power imbalance/coercion can produce agreement; fairness requires separate analysis.
Negotiation can be voluntary; coercion requires relevant pressure/threat conditions.
Bargaining power predicts influence, not normative legitimacy.
Having alternatives is distinct from coercive threats.
Mutual aid need not be transactional or immediately reciprocal.
Reciprocity can be relational and long-term rather than exact accounting.
Allocation by need does not create property rights.
Contribution can inform recognition/task roles without creating caste.
Agents can coordinate on shared goals while disagreeing elsewhere.

premises: A AND B AGREE_TO PLAN P
guards.reason: Plans/agreements can change under conditions, consent and governance.
Conflicts of interest/resources/interpretation can occur within cooperative relationships.
Mediation role does not inherently grant decision authority.
Collective action can coordinate diverse participants.
A coordination incentive problem does not establish a universal theory of agency.

invariants: Cooperation is a first-class strategy rather than an exception to presumed competition.
Cooperation requires compatible/shared aims, not identical preferences or identities.
Scarcity creates an allocation/coordination problem, not an automatic mandate for competition.
Negotiated agreement, factual truth and normative fairness remain distinct.
Bargaining power affects outcomes without establishing moral legitimacy.
Mutual aid, solidarity, commons governance, public provision, exchange and competition are distinct coordination mechanisms.
Shared-resource allocation never creates ownership or status merely through receipt/use.
Contribution does not create intrinsic rank or governance authority.
Conflict can occur inside healthy cooperative relationships without implying hostility.
Mediation assists coordination without automatically gaining authority to impose outcomes.
Collective action can preserve individual perspectives and dissent.
Agreements remain revisable under consent, changed conditions and governance.
Reciprocity need not become exact transactional accounting.
Cooperation and negotiation remain bounded by consent, privacy, authority and relationship boundaries.

provenance.authoring_basis: Cooperation theory, collective action, negotiation/mediation, commons governance, mutual aid, distributed coordination and Project Lantern's cooperative society-of-minds/economic-pluralism architecture.
